lesson.title: Estimating Slope When All You Have Is Data
lesson.summary: When a function is known only through a table of input-output pairs, the derivative at a point can be estimated using difference quotients formed from nearby table entries.
lesson.body:
Not every function in practice comes with a tidy formula. Sensor readings, survey results, and experimental measurements usually arrive as a table: a short list of input values paired with observed output values, with no algebraic rule connecting them. The derivative function still means the same thing in this setting, the instantaneous rate of change, but it has to be estimated using the limits from tables idea: since you cannot take h all the way to 0, you approximate the derivative using the smallest available h in the data, forming a difference quotient between adjacent table entries.

Suppose a table records the position of a moving object, in meters, at several times in seconds: at t = 1, position s = 2; at t = 2, position s = 8; at t = 3, position s = 18; at t = 4, position s = 32. To estimate the velocity, which is the derivative of position, at t = 2, there are two natural choices using only the table. The backward difference uses the interval from t = 1 to t = 2: (8 - 2) / (2 - 1) = 6 / 1 = 6 meters per second. The forward difference uses the interval from t = 2 to t = 3: (18 - 8) / (3 - 2) = 10 / 1 = 10 meters per second. These two estimates do not agree, 6 versus 10, because each one only looks in one direction from t = 2, the same limitation that shows up with one-sided derivatives.

It happens that this table comes from the exact formula s(t) = 2t^2, which can be checked directly: 2(1)^2 = 2, 2(2)^2 = 8, 2(3)^2 = 18, and 2(4)^2 = 32, matching every table entry. The true derivative is s'(t) = 4t, so the exact velocity at t = 2 is s'(2) = 8 meters per second. Notice that the backward estimate of 6 undershoots this true value, while the forward estimate of 10 overshoots it, and the true value of 8 sits exactly between them. This is not a coincidence: each one-sided estimate captures only half the curvature of the underlying motion, one lagging behind the true rate and one running ahead of it.

When working from a table, then, a forward difference and a backward difference are both legitimate estimates of the derivative at an interior point, but they generally disagree, and neither one is guaranteed to be more accurate than the other on its own. At the two ends of a table there is no choice at all: at the very first time listed, only a forward difference can be formed, and at the very last time listed, only a backward difference can be formed, since there is no earlier or later entry to pair it with. This mirrors the restriction built into limits from tables, where a limit near the edge of the available data can only be approached from whichever side has entries.

Real tables also rarely arrive with perfectly even spacing between inputs. If the times had instead been recorded at t = 1, 2, and 3.5, the backward difference from 2 to 1 would still use a step of 1, but a forward difference from 2 to 3.5 would use a step of 1.5, and the two resulting quotients would not be directly comparable in the same way. Whenever the spacing is uneven, it is worth explicitly writing the denominator as the actual gap between the two t-values used, rather than assuming a fixed step size, so the difference quotient still correctly reflects change in output over change in input.

The natural next question, given that the true value 8 fell right between the two one-sided estimates of 6 and 10 in this example, is whether combining both directions into a single estimate might do better than either alone. That combination is exactly the idea behind the symmetric difference quotient, taken up next.
